title: AI Agents Are Just Distributed Systems Now — Salman Munaf, TikTok

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk reframes the AI agent as a probabilistic coordinator and centers its architecture on the loop, boundaries, idempotent tools, retries, circuit breakers, scoped credentials, bound approvals, and recoverability — i.e., the harness around the model rather than the model itself.

secondary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk reframes the AI agent as a probabilistic coordinator and centers its architecture on the loop, boundaries, idempotent tools, retries, circuit breakers, scoped credentials, bound approvals, and recoverability — i.e., the harness around the model rather than the model itself.

summary:
Salman Munaf, a site reliability engineer at TikTok, argues that AI agents have crossed an architectural boundary the moment they began calling external services and producing side effects, and therefore must be treated as distributed systems. He opens with two cautionary incidents, the Replit agent deleting a production database and the Air Canada chatbot issuing an incorrect refund, both failures that basic systems thinking, such as scoped authority, backups, and authoritative source-of-truth retrieval, would have prevented.

He then walks through the agent loop (plan, act, observe, persist, decide) and shows that every step crosses a boundary into data sources, APIs, databases, or caches, each one a potential failure point. Because an agent is a probabilistic coordinator rather than a deterministic decision tree, all determinism must be enforced by surrounding controls. These controls include request IDs and idempotency keys on every tool call, status lookups when a call returns unknown, explicit compensating transactions for irreversible steps, and circuit breakers, exponential backoff, and ceilings on turns, parallelism, and spend to prevent retry storms and cascading failures.

Agent context is treated as state, not memory, with cache-style invalidation and provenance when the source of truth changes. Credentials must be scoped with separate read and write permissions, and human approvals must bind to action, timestamp, actor, and expiration so a $30 approval cannot silently authorize a $300 one. The talk closes by arguing that better models reduce mistakes but cannot eliminate network failures, stale data, or adversarial input; therefore teams must also reason about whether they can bound, observe, and recover from the agent's actions, capture full observability artifacts, enforce tool contracts with idempotency and schema, arbitrate conflicting memory against a source of truth, and ask what the system lets the agent do when it is wrong.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: AI agents are distributed systems the moment they call external services and produce side effects, so distributed-systems thinking must be applied from day one.
An agent is a probabilistic coordinator; determinism must be enforced by surrounding controls, not expected from the model itself.
A timeout means unknown, not failure, so every tool call needs request IDs, idempotency keys, and a status-lookup path to avoid duplicate side effects on retry.
Without explicit compensating transactions defined per step, partial multi-step agent workflows can leave downstream systems in inconsistent states.
Agent context is state, not memory: it must be treated as a cache with invalidation and provenance tied to the source of truth.
Retry storms, unbounded fan-out, and runaway spend require circuit breakers, exponential backoff, and hard ceilings on turns, parallelism, and cost.
Credentials must be scoped with separate read and write permissions, and human approvals must bind to action, timestamp, actor, and expiration.
Logs alone are insufficient; observability must capture the prompt, retrieved context, tool calls, responses, errors, writes, and approvals so failures can be reconstructed.
Better models reduce mistakes but cannot eliminate network failures, stale data, or adversarial input; the system must bound, observe, and recover from the agent's actions.
Reframe an AI agent as a probabilistic coordinator inside a distributed system and identify the boundaries it crosses

sections.title: Introduction: AI agents as distributed systems
sections.summary: Opens with a greeting and frames the talk: agents that call external systems are now distributed systems, so distributed-systems thinking is required. Two cautionary incidents (Replit deleting a production database, Air Canada chatbot issuing an incorrect refund) are cited as failures that good systems thinking would have caught, with scoped authority, robust backups, and authoritative source-of-truth retrieval as the missing controls.

sections.title: The architectural shift from chatbot to agent
sections.summary: Contrasts text-in/text-out chatbots with the agentic era, where models ingest prompts, run an agent loop, call tools, and cause side effects in the outside world. The architectural boundary now extends beyond the LLM itself, encompassing the external services, states, credentials, and actions involved.

sections.title: The agent as a probabilistic coordinator
sections.summary: Introduces the core reframe: where traditional workflow coordinators were deterministic decision trees, the AI agent is a probabilistic coordinator whose actions can vary widely and have severe consequences. Therefore deterministic controls must wrap the agent to constrain what it can do.

sections.title: The agent loop and boundary crossings
sections.summary: Walks through a typical plan, act, observe, persist, decide loop and shows that every step crosses a boundary (data sources, external APIs, databases, caches, retries). Argues for persisting every step so failures can be located and reversed, and for defining explicit compensating transactions per irreversible step such as an email sent to the wrong customer.

sections.title: Tool calls, timeouts, and idempotency
sections.summary: Treats tool calls as wrappers over remote APIs and databases that suffer network delays, timeouts, duplicate requests, and silent server-side success paired with client-reported errors. Uses a refund tool call timing out to argue that a timeout means unknown, not failure, and that request IDs, idempotency keys, and status lookups are required so retries do not produce duplicate side effects.

sections.title: Retries, budgets, and compensating actions
sections.summary: Notes that an agent's first instinct on failure is to retry, so idempotency must be baked in, retry storms must be prevented, and exponential backoff, max turns, max parallel calls, and max spend must be enforced. Compensation operations must be defined for any step that can produce side effects, including the case where a downstream system is updated and another such as the CRM is not.

sections.title: Context as state, not memory
sections.summary: Argues that context influencing action is state, so it goes stale, conflicts with authoritative data, or corrupts future actions. Distinguishes short-term (per execution thread) from long-term (project files, system prompts, databases, caches) memory and recommends treating memory as a cache with invalidation and provenance whenever the source of truth changes.

sections.title: Compensating actions across system boundaries
sections.summary: Reiterates that multi-step agent actions can succeed on early steps and fail later, so the entire transaction must be reversible, and these reversals can cross system boundaries. Gives the example of an incorrect customer email requiring a follow-up apology or correction message as the compensation operation.

sections.title: Circuit breakers, rate limits, and ceilings
sections.summary: Because the agent runs in a loop with retries, circuit breakers are needed to stop calls to unhealthy downstreams and prevent cascading failures. Rate limits and hard ceilings (max turns, max parallelism, max spend) are required so a stuck or thrashing agent cannot burn cost or saturate dependencies.

sections.title: Scoped credentials and bound human approval
sections.summary: Warns against handing agents blanket permissions; credentials should be scoped with separate read and write permissions and an allow-list of tools, since a harmless model becomes dangerous once it can perform unsafe operations. Human-in-the-loop approval must be bound to a specific action, timestamp, actor, and expiration, otherwise a $30 refund approval can silently authorize a $300 one.

sections.title: Observability beyond logs
sections.summary: Introduces observability as a hard requirement and argues logs alone are insufficient for reconstructing why an agent failed and what it was reacting to. Lists the artifacts that must be captured: the model called, the prompt given, retrieved context, the tool calls and their requests, responses and errors, the writes made, and the approvals obtained.

sections.title: Closing: bound, observe, and recover
sections.summary: Concludes that smarter models reduce mistakes and improve capability but cannot eliminate network failures, stale data, or adversarial input. Therefore the architecture must reason about whether it can bound, observe, and recover from the agent's actions. Calls for tool contracts that fix request/response schemas with idempotency baked in, source-of-truth arbitration when memory states conflict, retry policies and rate limits to prevent aggressive retrying, scoped permissions, traces, and recovery paths, and ends with the framing question: what does the system let the agent do when it is wrong?

demonstrations: Replit agent deleting a production database used as an example of missing backups and missing scoped authority
Air Canada chatbot issuing an incorrect refund used as an example of missing authoritative source-of-truth retrieval
Hypothetical refund tool call timing out to illustrate that a timeout means unknown, not failure, and that naive retry can double-refund a customer
Hypothetical $30 refund approval being reused to authorize a $300 refund to illustrate unbinding human approval from its parameters
limitations: Logs alone are not enough to reconstruct why an agent failed
Giving an agent blanket database privileges can turn a harmless model into a dangerous one
Retries without idempotency can cause duplicate side effects; retries without backoff or circuit breakers can cause cascading failures
Agent context can become stale, conflict with authoritative data, or corrupt future actions if treated as plain memory
Better models cannot eliminate network failures, stale data, or adversarial input
quantitativeClaims: $30 refund example vs. $300 unauthorized refund example used to show approval-binding failure
Examples reference 'max turns, max parallelism, max spend' as budget ceilings without specific numeric values
